name: Atari 7800 ProSystem
description: A console designed for Atari by General Computer Corporation, test-marketed in 1984 and shelved after the Tramiel takeover before a wide release in 1986. Its MARIA graphics chip could move many sprites, and it played nearly the whole 2600 library.
curiosities: It was the first Atari console to play almost all games for its predecessor without an adapter.
Some cartridges, such as Ballblazer, carried their own POKEY sound chip.
The CPU slows to about 1.19 MHz when it accesses TIA or RIOT.
NTSC 7800 cartridges carry a digital signature checked by the BIOS at boot.
It was the first Atari console designed outside the company, by General Computer Corporation.
During development it was called the Atari 3600.
It launched nationwide in May 1986 at US$79.95.
It came with a two-button Pro-Line joystick; Europe got a joypad that America never saw.
A High Score Cartridge that saved scores for up to 65 games was cancelled; nine games support it.
Later models dropped the expansion port meant for a LaserDisc player.
PAL consoles skip the signature check and recognise 7800 cartridges by other means, because of export rules on encryption.
The signing software was found and released at the Classic Gaming Expo in 2001.
Only 59 official games came out for it.
Five games work with the XG-1 light gun, among them Barnyard Blaster and Alien Brigade.
In 2024 Atari brought out the Atari 7800+, a smaller copy of the European model.

story: Atari commissioned General Computer Corporation, who had made Ms. Pac-Man, to build its next console; the 7800 was ready in 1984 and played 2600 games too.

Then Atari was sold to Jack Tramiel, who put it on the shelf; it only launched in 1986, against the NES. Its graphics chip could move many sprites, but its sound was the 2600's. Food Fight, Ninja Golf and Midnight Mutants were among its games.
About a million units were sold before it ended in 1992; its homebrew scene is lively today.
